ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Wilderness and Expedition Medicine Referral — Robert Falcon Scott — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient pre-expedition medical assessment before a long Antarctic expedition: history, examination, ECG, blood tests, mental health and alcohol screening, an elevated blood pressure, tobacco counseling, and a wilderness and expedition medicine referral

text.paragraph: Pre-expedition assessment of a 41-year-old naval officer who will lead a long Antarctic expedition sailing in about five months, with a winter in a hut and sledge journeys of several months on foot. Please advise on his fitness and any further testing, the management of a newly raised blood pressure in that setting, nutrition and scurvy prevention, cold injury and altitude precautions, mental health and sleep in isolation, and an evacuation and communication plan. [S]

list.item: Is he fit for a long polar expedition with heavy sledge hauling, and does he need any further cardiac or other testing?
If his blood pressure is confirmed as raised, how and when should it be treated, given cold, dehydration and long marches?
What nutrition plan, including energy and vitamin C, will prevent the scurvy and weight loss of his earlier journey?
What frostbite, hypothermia and altitude precautions and training does the party need?
How should his mental health and sleep be supported in months of isolation and polar light?
What evacuation, communication and medical kit plan is appropriate?

text.paragraph: Well and fully active, with no cardiac or respiratory symptoms. Office blood pressure 144/90 mmHg today; one week of home readings requested to confirm. Pipe smoker, about 25 g of tobacco a week since his early twenties; varenicline started today with a quit date in one week. Alcohol within low-risk limits (AUDIT-C 3). On a long polar sledge journey in his mid-thirties he had scurvy, with red gums and swollen ankles and legs, which improved on fresh seal meat, and he had weeks of lassitude after returning; he recovered fully. Examination: BMI 24.2, heart and lungs normal, no edema. ECG: sinus rhythm, no left ventricular hypertrophy. Sodium 140 and potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL (eGFR 107), fasting glucose 92 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.3%, total cholesterol 196, HDL 52, LDL 122 and triglycerides 110 mg/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL. PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4. Dental, hearing and eye checks are being arranged. He is anxious that nothing should stop him leading the sledge journeys himself [S]

list.item: He wants nothing found that would keep him from leading the sledge journeys himself. [S]
He remembers scurvy and weeks of exhaustion after his last long sledge journey and wants the expedition's food and medical plan to prevent it. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Robert Falcon Scott was born on June 6, 1868, at Plymouth, Devon, into a seafaring family, and joined his first Royal Navy ship when he was 13. [D]
He led the Discovery expedition to the Antarctic from 1901 to 1904. [D]

In October 1902, at the Discovery's winter quarters, scurvy was found after a sledge party returned from the western journey; the expedition's surgeon then examined everyone on board and found signs in a good many men, in most only the merest indication, and the outbreak was over by about October 20. Scott arranged to replace part of the sledging pemmican with cooked seal meat. [D]

On the southern sledge journey (November 1902 to February 1903) the party examined gums and legs every Sunday. When one companion developed angry-looking gums in late December 1902, they stopped eating bacon and increased the seal-meat ration, and Scott recorded that the scurvy symptoms lessened. [D]

At a thorough medical examination on the southern journey on January 14, 1903, Scott recorded that he himself had "distinctly red gums, and a very slight swelling in the ankles." Two days later, on a double ration of seal meat, his gums were much cleaner and his leg vastly improved; by the last days of the journey he wrote that their scurvy had been advancing again and that his ankles were considerably swollen. [D]

After the southern party returned to the ship in February 1903, Scott wrote that he had both legs much swollen and very uncomfortable gums, and an extraordinary lassitude, physical and mental, that lasted many weeks before he returned to a normally vigorous condition. [D]

In his account of the Discovery expedition he wrote that scurvy was then believed to be ptomaine poisoning from tainted meat. A modern historian of medicine notes that many British doctors of the time accepted this view and overlooked the experiments of Holst and Frølich on dietary deficiency, so medical advice given to him before his second expedition would probably not have helped him prevent scurvy. [R]
On the southern journey, on December 20, 1902, he wrote that his tobacco supply was so low that he had been trying tea leaves, which were "nothing less than horrid." [D]

After the Discovery expedition the needs of the naval service called him to the command of battleships and to confidential work at the Admiralty, and five years passed before he resumed Antarctic work. In 1908 he married the sculptor Kathleen Bruce; they had one son. [D]

On November 24, 1909, he wrote from the offices of the British Antarctic Expedition at 36 and 38 Victoria Street, London, that the Pole was at the forefront of the campaign for raising funds but that scientific work would not be neglected. [D]

list.item: Naval officer and polar explorer; leading a scientific expedition to the Antarctic that sails in about five months, with a voyage south, a winter in a hut, and sledge journeys of several months on foot; for much of the year no evacuation is possible [S]
Married, with a young son; lives in London and works long days raising funds and organizing the expedition [S]
Tobacco: smokes a pipe, about 25 g of tobacco a week, more on long working days, since his early twenties; first pipe within an hour of waking; no cigarettes [S]
Alcohol: a glass or two of wine with dinner on three or four evenings a week (AUDIT-C 3); no other drugs [S]
Exercise: walks fast across London every day; no regular endurance or strength training since his last expedition [S]
Sleep: six to seven hours, shorter when the expedition work presses; no snoring reported [S]

Confirm the blood pressure with a validated upper-arm home monitor, two readings morning and evening for seven days, and start lifestyle measures: less salt, more fruit and vegetables, regular endurance training, and alcohol within limits. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (Jones DW, et al. Circulation 2025;152(11):e114-e218) (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension monograph (2026) [S]

Stop pipe tobacco: varenicline with a quit date in one week, counseling at each visit, and the quitline; nicotine products avoided because nicotine narrows skin blood vessels and adds to frostbite risk. Guideline: Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Frostbite: 2024 Update (McIntosh SE, et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2024;35(2):183-197) (2024); Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]

Baseline PHQ-9 and GAD-7 before a long isolated expedition, repeated before departure, with a mental health and sleep support plan. Guideline: Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023); Anxiety Disorders in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
Dental examination and cleaning, pure-tone audiometry, and an eye examination with a spare pair of glasses before departure. Guideline: USPSTF A and B Recommendations (2026) [S]
Referral to wilderness and expedition medicine, Sebastian Nwankwo-Lund, MD, ordered 1910-01-13 [S]
